sm: The host opens a conversation with a guest who first did anthropological fieldwork on the Indonesian island of Flores in 1984. The Homo floresiensis remains were found in 2003 and announced in 2004. The guest says that on his first visit he heard local stories of small humanlike creatures, including one group said to have died out about 230 years earlier. Later he heard of similar creatures in the Lio region to the east, which he writes about in his book. He distinguishes the fossil species from the creatures Lio people say are still rare but present. He also describes older teeth and jaw fragments, about 700,000 years old, found near pygmy stegodon bones, and notes that ambiguous stone tools cannot be tied to a species without skeletal evidence.

The guest explains that recent studies suggest the pygmy stegodons were probably killed by Komodo dragons, with some marks possibly from stone tools used to scrape meat. Modern humans on Flores are now dated to around 50,000 years ago, overlapping with floresiensis, which was first thought to be only 12,000 or 13,000 years old. He compares the legend to the Orang Pendek of Sumatra, but says Flores has no native apes or monkeys, so there are no primates to be mistaken for a small human. The sightings come almost entirely from the mountain forests of the Lio region, far from settlements. He recorded over 30 reports, about a dozen of them quite interesting, while the less credible ones were near the coast and could have been monkeys.
